profile.summary: CellBench is an evaluation of single-cell foundation models used as frozen feature extractors, that is with their weights unchanged and only a light head fitted on top. The authors compare 13 such models with classical methods fitted on the training data itself, across 12 human and mouse cohorts and four genetic perturbation screens. Their reported conclusions are that different models preserve different biological information, that classical baselines stay competitive, that human-pretrained representations transfer to supervised mouse analyses but under a shared decoder none beats simply predicting no change for unseen perturbation targets, and that neither model size nor reported pretraining data volume predicts performance. This page is written from the abstract and metadata alone, because the preprint's full text is on bioRxiv, which this run was not allowed to request.

summary_quotes.text: Here, we present CellBench, a unified benchmark of frozen scFM representations across tissues, species, and genetic perturbation screens.
CellBench compares 13 frozen single-cell foundation models with classical baselines fitted on training data across 12 human and mouse cohorts and four genetic perturbation screens.
We find that different models capture distinct aspects of cellular biology, while classical baselines remain competitive across tasks.

Human-pretrained representations transfer to supervised mouse analyses, but under a shared decoder they fail to improve genome-wide absolute error over predicting no change for unseen perturbation targets.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: What a single-cell foundation model's embedding keeps, and whether it is worth using instead of a method fitted on the data at hand. The authors frame the open question as which biological information the embeddings preserve and when the models beat dataset-fitted methods. Two kinds of task are distinguished in the abstract: representing observed cellular states, which the authors treat as the observational side, and predicting how cells respond to genetic interventions, which they report as a different matter where success on the first does not carry over. A third question is evidential rather than biological: whether a model's apparent advantage survives the removal of cohorts that overlap its own pretraining records.

quotes.text: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for transcriptomic analysis, yet it remains unclear what biological information their embeddings preserve and when they outper- form dataset-fitted methods.
It also reveals an important distinction between representing observed cellular states and predicting how cells respond to genetic interventions.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The abstract gives the shape of the data and nothing more: 12 human and mouse cohorts, covering tissues and species, and four genetic perturbation screens. The comparison set is 13 frozen foundation models against classical baselines that are fitted on the training data. The perturbation side is said to include unseen perturbation targets. Nothing in the material that could be fetched names the cohorts, the cell counts, the gene sets, the screens or the splits, so none of those is stated here.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Three things can be said from the abstract. First, the backbones are frozen, so what is evaluated is the representation rather than a fine-tuned model, and the comparison is against methods fitted on the training data. Second, the perturbation task is scored on genome-wide absolute error against an explicit reference of predicting no change, and the authors report that under a shared decoder no model improves on that reference for unseen targets. Third, a sensitivity analysis removes cohorts whose sample or donor identifiers match a model's pretraining records, and the authors report that this reduces the annotation advantages while leaving the model rankings largely unchanged. The metrics for the other tasks, the aggregation across cohorts, the number of seeds and the exact splits are not in the material that could be fetched.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Frozen backbones with a fitted head. The foundation models are evaluated as frozen representations, so they are not fine-tuned, and the perturbation task uses a decoder shared across models. The record's own earlier note describes the setting as zero-shot representation for clustering and batch correction with lightweight fine-tuning of task-specific heads for the other tasks, but that wording comes from an earlier version's abstract and is not in the text fetched here.

strengths.text: The comparison includes methods fitted on the data at hand, and the authors report that those remain competitive, which is the comparison a reader needs before adopting a foundation model.

notes: Coverage is limited and deliberately so. The record's two attached sources are bioRxiv pages for the same DOI, https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.04.01.714123v1 and the v2 address; this run was told not to request bioRxiv, and the saved Europe PMC record PPR1216366 marks the preprint isOpenAccess N and inPMC N, so the full text was not available. The page is therefore written from the Europe PMC core record's title, author list, date and structured abstract only. One doubt for a human, the name: Europe PMC serves this DOI as CellBench: task-dependent performance and generalization limits of single-cell foundation models, while the store holds CellBench-LS from v1 and a different v2 title, so the record's name, task field and scope note come from abstracts that the current version has replaced. The released date 2026-04-05 is the Europe PMC first publication date for the preprint.
